explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD says, “Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins.” (Isaiah 17:1) That's not a city with a few cracks in the wall. I've seen a cookie sheet hit the floor with more left standing than that.

A city of refuge sounds cozy, but that's not what the LORD says here. He says Damascus is no longer a city at all. It has become a heap of ruins (Isaiah 17:1). A pile of rubble isn't taking in guests.

Palm trees would be a nice upgrade, friend, but the verse never goes there. The LORD says Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins (Isaiah 17:1). Just rubble. Nobody's booking a vacation to that skyline.

That's right. The cities of Aroer are forsaken, and the verse says they “…will be left to the flocks, which will lie down with no one to fear.” (Isaiah 17:2) Think about that for a second. The new tenants are animals, and they're about the most relaxed neighbors a street ever had.
Jackals sound dramatic, I'll give you that. But the verse doesn't mention them. It says the cities of Aroer “…will be left to the flocks…” (Isaiah 17:2). Calmer crowd, friend.

You might expect a new crowd of people to move in. But the verse doesn't say that. It says the forsaken cities of Aroer “…will be left to the flocks, which will lie down with no one to fear.” (Isaiah 17:2) The flocks get the whole place, and they lie down with no one to fear.

You got it, baker. The LORD of Hosts declares, “The remnant of Aram will be like the splendor of the Israelites…” (Isaiah 17:3). I'm not going to guess what that comparison means, because the verse doesn't spell it out. I'll just point at what it says and keep my mustache still.

Egypt is a famous name, so I see why it jumped out. But the verse never brings it up. The LORD of Hosts says, “The remnant of Aram will be like the splendor of the Israelites…” (Isaiah 17:3). The comparison is with Israel, friend.

Babylon's a big name, and big names love to crash a verse. This one doesn't have them, though. The LORD of Hosts says, “The remnant of Aram will be like the splendor of the Israelites…” (Isaiah 17:3). The comparison is with the Israelites, plain and simple.
Yes, fade. The LORD says, “In that day the splendor of Jacob will fade…” (Isaiah 17:4). Think of my apron after way too many washes. The splendor was there, and then it starts to go.

Shine is a happy word, so I get the pull. But the LORD says the opposite: “In that day the splendor of Jacob will fade…” (Isaiah 17:4). This verse is on the dim side, friend. The splendor goes down, not up.

Return would be a comeback story, but this verse isn't telling one. The LORD says, “In that day the splendor of Jacob will fade…” (Isaiah 17:4). The word is fade. No coming back is mentioned in that line.
True! The LORD says, “Yet gleanings will remain…” (Isaiah 17:6). The reaper has been through, but something is still left behind. Even after a hard sweep, the text points to what remains.
It's true, friend. The LORD says, “Yet gleanings will remain…” (Isaiah 17:6). The reaper has done his work, and still the text says something is left. Don't count the field empty.

That's right, friend. “In that day men will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 17:7) After all that ruin, the eyes finally go up. The very next verse says they will not look to the altars they have fashioned with their hands. I love when somebody looks at the right One.

Kings are a natural guess, since verse 3 says the sovereignty will disappear from Damascus. But verse 7 never mentions them. It says men “…will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel.” (Isaiah 17:7) The eyes go to the One who made them.

Close to the neighborhood, friend, but it's the opposite. The very next verse says they will not look to the altars they have fashioned with their hands (Isaiah 17:8). In that day, men “…will look to their Maker…” (Isaiah 17:7). The Maker gets the look, not something they made.

I can see why you'd say that, but it's the other way around. The text says, “They will not look to the altars they have fashioned with their hands…” (Isaiah 17:8). The eyes that turn to the Maker stop looking at what hands built. So that statement is false.

False is right. “They will not look to the altars they have fashioned with their hands…” (Isaiah 17:8). They turned their eyes to their Maker in the verse before. Once you're looking up, you're not staring at your own handiwork.

Yes. “For you have forgotten the God of your salvation…” (Isaiah 17:10). The next part says they also failed to remember the Rock of their refuge. Forgetting is easy, friend. I've forgotten where I put my own mixing spoon, but this is a much bigger thing to lose track of.

Followed sounds like the right direction, but it's not the word here. The message says, “For you have forgotten the God of your salvation…” (Isaiah 17:10). It's about forgetting. It's not about following.

Feared is a reasonable guess, but the verse uses a different word. It says, “For you have forgotten the God of your salvation…” (Isaiah 17:10). The trouble in that line is forgetting. The next part says they also failed to remember the Rock of their refuge.

Right. “…yet the harvest will vanish on the day of disease and incurable pain.” (Isaiah 17:11) The verses before it say they cultivate delightful plots and set out cuttings from exotic vines. All that planting and tending, and then it's gone. That's about the saddest empty tray I can picture.

Locusts are a classic harvest villain, but this verse doesn't name them. It says, “…yet the harvest will vanish on the day of disease and incurable pain.” (Isaiah 17:11) The harvest vanishes. That's the word the text gives us.

explanations.answer: a flood will sweep it away
explanations.explanation: A flood is a dramatic way for a harvest to go, but the verse doesn't mention one. It says, “…yet the harvest will vanish on the day of disease and incurable pain.” (Isaiah 17:11) The word is vanish. Nothing is said about water in that line.
I get why you'd think so, since they were roaring like the sea a moment ago. But the text says, “He rebukes them, and they flee far away…” (Isaiah 17:13). They don't hold the line. They run.

False is right, baker. “He rebukes them, and they flee far away…” (Isaiah 17:13). All that rumbling like mighty waters, and when the rebuke comes, they run. Nobody is planting their feet in that verse.
Yes! “In the evening, there is sudden terror! Before morning, they are no more!” (Isaiah 17:14) Sudden terror comes in the evening. Before morning, they're gone. That's all inside one night.

A whole week would be a long wait, and the verse doesn't give one. It says, “In the evening, there is sudden terror! Before morning, they are no more!” (Isaiah 17:14) The timing is one night, friend. They don't last until sunrise.

Waiting until the next harvest isn't in the verse. “In the evening, there is sudden terror! Before morning, they are no more!” (Isaiah 17:14) Evening to morning, friend. The text puts it before morning, all inside a single night.

True. The message says, “This is the portion of those who loot us and the lot of those who plunder us.” (Isaiah 17:14) That's how the passage ends, with a clear word about what happens to them. Short, sharp, and nothing added.

It's actually true, friend. The message says, “This is the portion of those who loot us and the lot of those who plunder us.” (Isaiah 17:14) That's the very last line of the passage. The sudden end belongs to the ones who loot and plunder.
